summary: Describes the UTF-16 encoding of Unicode and ISO 10646, how to serialize it as bytes for transmission, and the MIME charset naming and registration. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: UTF-16 turns Unicode character numbers into 16-bit units and then into bytes. A label or a marker at the start tells a reader which byte order to use.

questions: how is utf-16 sent over the internet
what is a byte order mark
subtitle: How UTF-16 represents Unicode characters and labels their byte order.

tldr.problem: Programs need a shared way to encode Unicode character values as bytes. A receiver also needs to know the order of the bytes in each 16-bit value.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-16 uses one 16-bit value for character values below 0x10000 and a pair of surrogate values for values from 0x10000 through 0x10FFFF. Charset labels and an optional byte-order mark identify serialization order.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes UTF-16 serialization and registers the labels UTF-16BE, UTF-16LE and UTF-16. It is Informational and does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2781 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: UTF-16 and Character Values
sections.content:
RFC 2781 describes UTF-16, an encoding of Unicode and ISO 10646 character data. Each character has a number, called its character value in the memo, and UTF-16 represents that number as one or two unsigned 16-bit integers.

Values below 0x10000 use one integer. Values from 0x10000 through 0x10FFFF use two integers called a high surrogate and a low surrogate. Values above 0x10FFFF cannot be encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: Most character values use one 16-bit number. Larger values use a pair of numbers that the reader must interpret together.

sections.title: Encoding and Decoding Surrogate Pairs
sections.content:
To encode a value above 0xFFFF, UTF-16 subtracts 0x10000 and divides the remaining 20 bits between two 16-bit units. The first unit is in the high-surrogate range 0xD800 to 0xDBFF; the second is in the low-surrogate range 0xDC00 to 0xDFFF.

When decoding, a high surrogate must be followed by a low surrogate. An unpaired surrogate or an invalid pair is an error. The RFC does not specify error recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: A character that needs two UTF-16 units must use them in the right order: high surrogate first, low surrogate second. A missing or wrong partner makes the sequence invalid.

sections.title: Byte Order and the BOM
sections.content:
A 16-bit integer can be serialized with its higher-order byte first (big-endian) or lower-order byte first (little-endian). The byte order mark (BOM) is the character value 0xFEFF placed at the beginning of a stream to signal the byte order.

In a UTF-16 stream, initial bytes 0xFE 0xFF indicate big-endian order and 0xFF 0xFE indicate little-endian order. Away from the start of a stream, 0xFEFF is a character, not a BOM.
sections.plainLanguage: Two bytes can be written in either order. A marker at the beginning can tell the reader which order was used; the same character elsewhere is ordinary text.

sections.title: Choosing a MIME Charset Label
sections.content:
The memo registers three labels. UTF-16BE means big-endian and UTF-16LE means little-endian; neither label uses a BOM. UTF-16 leaves the order open, so a sender SHOULD begin with a BOM and a reader MUST inspect the first two octets to determine the order.

If a UTF-16-labeled stream has no BOM, a reader SHOULD interpret it as big-endian. The memo also says these labels are not suitable for MIME media types under the top-level text type, with an HTTP exception.
sections.plainLanguage: Use UTF-16BE or UTF-16LE when the byte order is known. Use UTF-16 when the reader must check the beginning of the data to learn the order.

sections.title: Handling Untrusted Text
sections.content:
The RFC warns that text can contain unknown characters, control characters or special characters that trigger external processing. A processor should handle those values without harming the recipient or running embedded code without warning.

Implementations also need to handle invalid UTF-16 sequences carefully. An attacker could send malformed byte sequences to exploit a parser that behaves unexpectedly.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs should treat text as data, not automatically run it as instructions. They also need to detect broken surrogate pairs rather than processing them unsafely.
